introduction: This level targets 3-phase AC machines, specifically focusing on the Rotating Magnetic Field (RMF), Synchronous Speed calculations, and the critical concept of 'Slip' in Induction Motors.

core_concepts.title: Synchronous Speed ($N_s$)
core_concepts.description:
The speed at which the Rotating Magnetic Field (RMF) created by the stator windings revolves in the air gap. 
Formula: **$N_s = \frac{120f}{P}$** (Where $f$ = supply frequency in Hz, $P$ = number of poles).

core_concepts.title: Slip ($s$) and Rotor Frequency
core_concepts.description:
The rotor of an induction motor can never catch up to the synchronous speed ($N_s$); it always rotates at a slightly lesser speed ($N_r$). This relative difference is the slip.
Formula: **$s = \frac{N_s - N_r}{N_s}$** 
**Rotor Frequency ($f_r$):** The frequency of the induced current in the rotor is directly proportional to the slip: **$f_r = s \times f$**.

core_concepts.title: Types of Induction Motor Rotors
core_concepts.description:
1. **Squirrel Cage Rotor:** The most common, rugged, and cheap design. Bars are permanently short-circuited via end rings. External resistance *cannot* be added.
2. **Slip Ring (Wound) Rotor:** Features an external slip ring mechanism allowing external resistance to be added to the rotor circuit, which drastically improves starting torque.

important_entities.name: Motor Starters
important_entities.significance: When switched on, a 3-phase induction motor draws a dangerously high starting current (5 to 7 times the full-load current). Starters (like Star-Delta or Autotransformer) are used primarily to reduce this starting voltage and limit the initial current surge.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
Exam Trap: Examiners frequently ask for the slip when the motor is just starting (at standstill). 
When the motor is stationary, rotor speed $N_r = 0$. 
Therefore, **$s = \frac{N_s - 0}{N_s} = 1$**. 
At standstill, Slip = 1 (or 100%), and the rotor frequency equals the supply frequency ($f_r = f$).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always remember that speed ($N_s$) is directly proportional to frequency ($f$) and inversely proportional to the number of poles ($P$).

exam_strategy_tips: A standard State AE/JE numerical: 'A 4-pole, 3-phase induction motor operates on a 50 Hz supply. What is its synchronous speed?' Answer: $(120 \times 50) / 4 = 1500$ RPM.
